newsitem.title: BURMA: Military lifts roadblocks, puts tanks in Rangoon.
newsitem.headline: Military lifts roadblocks, puts tanks in Rangoon.

text.p: Burma's military rulers displayed confidence on Friday by lifting most roadblocks near two troubled city universities after student protestors failed to regroup and stage new street demonstrations.

At the same time, the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) stationed five army tanks in front of Rangoon's city hall, signalling it would crush any fresh protests, diplomats and witnesses told Reuters.

Diplomats said they were puzzled by conflicting security measures taken by the SLORC, but noted the move might have been in response to rumours that some students planned to stage an anti-government demonstration in the area.
The tanks were near a public square facing the city hall and the adjoining Sule Pagoda, which has been closed to tourists since earlier this week in an unprecedent move.

"The lifting of the roadblocks is a show that they are in firm control but the presence of armoured vehicles is a conflicting sign, indicating that the situation is still unpredictable," one diplomat told Reuters.
Students at the two campuses had chanted anti-government slogans inside their compounds earlier this week.
Top SLORC leaders had warned on Thursday in the official media that they would not tolerate any new disturbances.
Thousands of students from the Yangon Institute of Technology and the Yangon University led streets protests in Rangoon last week, demanding more freedom and rights and condemning police brutality.
The military detained more than 860 protestors but later freed them.
The protests were the worst seen in Rangoon since September 1988 when student-led pro-democracy demonstrations were crushed by the military, leaving thousands dead or in jail.

On Thursday, a member of opposition leader Aung San Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) said the government had arrested 28 NLD members between December 7 and 11 in connection with a street protest by students.

NLD deputy secretary-general U Tin Oo said the arrested NLD members were onlookers at the protests. Six NLD members were later released, but one laundry worker not linked to the NLD died after being beaten during the demonstration.
A government spokesman said on Friday that fewer than 10 NLD members had been arrested for being suspected agitators during the protest and that the government had evidence against them.
Earlier this week, the spokesman charged that some NLD members along with some exiled Burmese students and the outlawed Communist Party of Burma had instigated the student protests.
"The arrests (of the NLD members) look like the government is trying to pin the blame on the party," a diplomat said.
Some diplomats said they had been advised by the Burmese Foreign Ministry to stay away from further student protests.

The government spokesman said the request was not meant to suggest that some embassies were involved in the protests but as a safety tip for diplomats who might be near protest sites to follow the situation.

"Some embassy officials may go out to gather information for their reports to their governments. We have no problems with that, but if something happens to them, it would be difficult for anyone to help them," he said.
